solution:
Molar conductivity and conductivity are related by \(\Lambda = \dfrac{1000\,k}{c}\). Writing this for both solutions and dividing,

\(\dfrac{\Lambda_1}{\Lambda_2} = \dfrac{k_1}{k_2} \times \dfrac{c_2}{c_1} = \dfrac{k_1/k_2}{c_1/c_2}\)

The ratio of conductivities is \(k_1/k_2 = 0.216\) and the ratio of concentrations is \(c_1/c_2 = 0.4\). Hence

\(\dfrac{\Lambda_1}{\Lambda_2} = \dfrac{0.216}{0.4} = 0.54\)

The other three values are the remaining ways of combining the same two numbers, and each corresponds to a wrong placement of \(c\) in the formula : \(0.216 \times 0.4 = 0.0864\) (multiplying instead of dividing), \(0.4/0.216 = 1.852\) (inverting the ratio) and \(1/(0.216 \times 0.4) = 11.574\). Only \(0.54\) follows from \(\Lambda = 1000k/c\).

Conductivity \(k\) is the conductance of ions present in \(1\ \mathrm{cm^3}\) of solution, so it depends on the number of ions per unit volume. On dilution the total number of ions does increase (the degree of dissociation rises), but not in proportion to the dilution, so the number of ions **per unit volume** falls and \(k\) DECREASES.

Molar conductivity \(\Lambda\) is the conductance due to the ions furnished by 1 mole of electrolyte, however large the volume needed to hold that mole. Dilution increases the number of ions produced by that one mole, so \(\Lambda\) INCREASES.

So the two quantities move in opposite senses, which rules out both "both increase" and "both decrease"; and the remaining pair is distinguished by which one falls — it is \(k\), the per-volume quantity, not \(\Lambda\), the per-mole quantity.

Convert only the area unit, since S and \(\Omega^{-1}\) are the same unit and \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\) is common to both sides.

\(1\ \mathrm{m^2} = (100\ \mathrm{cm})^2 = 10^4\ \mathrm{cm^2}\)

Therefore \(1\ \mathrm{S\ m^2\ mol^{-1}} = 10^{4}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}} = 10^{4}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\).

The alternative with \(10^{-4}\) is dimensionally the same unit as the quantity itself, so it can only be true if the numerical factor were 1; \(10^{-2}\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) and \(10^{2}\ \Omega^{-1}\ \mathrm{cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) both use a linear conversion \((10^{\pm 2})\) where an AREA needs the square of it.

In the given reaction \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is oxidised to \(\mathrm{H^\oplus}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\) is reduced to \(\mathrm{Cu}\). So the hydrogen electrode is the anode and the copper electrode the cathode.

\(E^0_{cell} = E^0_{\text{cathode}} - E^0_{\text{anode}} = E^0_{Cu} - E^0_{\mathrm{H^\oplus/H_2}}\)

Because \(\mathrm{H_2}\) is at 1 atm and \(\mathrm{H^\oplus}\) at 1 M, the anode is the standard hydrogen electrode, whose potential is defined as zero. Hence

\(E^0_{cell} = 0.34\ \mathrm{V} - 0 = 0.34\ \mathrm{V}\)

The value \(-0.34\) V would follow only if the cell were written in reverse, and the two values \(\pm 0.17\) V come from dividing by the two electrons transferred — but cell potential is an intensive property and is never divided by \(n\).

The cell reaction is \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + 2\mathrm{Ag^\oplus(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}(aq)} + 2\mathrm{Ag(s)}\), with \(n = 2\), and the Nernst equation gives

\(E_{cell} = E^0_{cell} - \dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2}\log_{10}\dfrac{[\mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}}]}{[\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}]^2}\)

The anode compartment holds \(\mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}}\), which is in the NUMERATOR of the reaction quotient. Multiplying it by 10 raises \(\log_{10}Q\) by exactly 1, so

\(\Delta E = -\dfrac{0.0592\ \mathrm{V}}{2} \times 1 = -0.0296\ \mathrm{V}\)

i.e. the emf falls by 0.0296 V. The sign settles the choice between the two 0.0296 V options — a larger product concentration always lowers the emf — and the two "10 V" options confuse the factor of 10 in the concentration with a change in volts.

In a table of reduction half reactions the species on the LEFT are oxidising agents and those on the RIGHT are reducing agents. Oxidising strength increases with \(E^0\); reducing strength increases as \(E^0\) becomes more negative.

The largest \(E^0\) here is \(0.8\) V, so the strongest oxidising agent is the left-side species of that half reaction, \(\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\). The most negative \(E^0\) is \(-0.44\) V, so the strongest reducing agent is the right-side species of that half reaction, \(\mathrm{Fe}\).

Each of the other three pairs fails on one half or the other : \(\mathrm{Ag}\) is the reduced form and so cannot be an oxidising agent at all, while \(\mathrm{Fe^{2\oplus}}\) is the OXIDISING agent of the \(-0.44\) V couple, not its reducing agent; \(\mathrm{Pb^{2\oplus}}\) has only the third-largest \(E^0\); and \(\mathrm{I_2}\) at \(0.53\) V is a weaker oxidising agent than \(\mathrm{Ag^\oplus}\) at \(0.8\) V.

Balancing the reaction shows that 2 moles of electrons are transferred, so \(n = 2\). Then

\(\Delta G^0 = -n\mathrm{F}E^0_{cell} = -2 \times 96500\ \mathrm{C\ mol^{-1}} \times 0.57\ \mathrm{V}\)

\(= -110010\ \mathrm{J} \approx -110\ \mathrm{kJ}\)

The sign is not a matter of convention here : \(E^0_{cell}\) is positive, so the reaction is spontaneous and \(\Delta G^0\) must be negative — that rules out both \(+110\) kJ and \(+55\) kJ. The magnitude \(55\) kJ is what \(n = 1\) would give, but two electrons pass from \(\mathrm{Ni}\) to \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\).

The question asks which statement is NOT correct.

Gibbs energy is proportional to the amount of substance, so it is an extensive property — that statement is correct. Electrode and cell potentials do not depend on how much material is present, so they are intensive — also correct. And the maximum electrical work obtainable from a cell is \(W = -\Delta G\), which is the correct relation.

The remaining statement is the false one : because \(E^0\) is INTENSIVE, multiplying a half reaction by a numerical factor does not change its \(E^0\). What is multiplied is \(n\), and hence \(\Delta G^0 = -n\mathrm{F}E^0\), which is extensive. Claiming that \(E^0\) scales with the factor also contradicts the statement two lines above it, which the question itself presents as correct.

During discharge the lead storage cell delivers current, so oxidation occurs at the \(\mathrm{Pb}\) plate (the anode) and electrons must be RELEASED, that is, they must appear on the product side.

\(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{PbSO_4(s)} + 2\mathrm{e^\ominus}\)

Of the alternatives, one shows electrons being consumed and is therefore a reduction — that is the cathode reaction of discharge, not an oxidation. Another is the reverse of the \(\mathrm{PbO_2}\) cathode reaction and so belongs to RECHARGING rather than discharge. The last involves no electron transfer at all, so it is not a half reaction of the cell.

By Kohlrausch law of independent migration of ions, the molar conductivity at zero concentration is the sum of the molar ionic conductivities, each weighted by the NUMBER of that ion produced by one formula unit.

One formula unit of \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) gives 2 \(\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}\) ions and 3 \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}\) ions, so

\(\Lambda_0 = 2\,\lambda^0_{\mathrm{Al^{3\oplus}}} + 3\,\lambda^0_{\mathrm{SO_4^{2\ominus}}}\)

The expression with coefficients 3 and 2 has the two subscripts interchanged; the one with \(1/3\) and \(1/2\) uses the reciprocals of the ionic charges instead of the stoichiometric numbers; and the one with unit coefficients would be correct only for a 1 : 1 electrolyte.
